meta.title: BubbleWrap your dev env and agents
meta.author: dpc_pw

comments.author: altano
comments.text:
This is baked into Claude Code fwiw: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#os-level-enforcement (Seatbelt on macOS and BubbleWrap on Linux).

I've been playing with the sandboxing and it sort of works. The network isolation is too restrictive, since it works by domain. I can't allow ssh to hit an IP, for example. But you can add escape hatches for some commands, and then those don't go through the sandbox.

I used to carefully read every single command before executing and now I can be a little more cavalier. Not a lot more cavalier, mind you, since there are still lots of dangerous network operations claude could execute to mess up my remote systems. But if something is just reading or writing to my local system I can blindly accept with confidence knowing that it can only do so within the parameters of my sandbox.

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text:
Notably, in my setup I am also sandboxing the terminal tmux tabs I'm opening to work on a project. I'm e.g. concerned about Slopus writing code that is subtly but critically wrong, which I would then execute, possibly semi-automatically (direnvs, etc.).

I'm also concerned with Slopus just reading stuff that it shouldn't. I also don't trust built in isolation on principle. That thing is not an Open Source code, it can say whatever it wants and do something slightly different.  As I know the layout of my home directory, I (and anyone) can make much better job at only exposing what is really necessary. Who knows when the monetization strategies are going to change, etc. Also - the governments and agencies might want to spy etc.

comments.author: thesadsre
comments.text: The problem is that Claude code has also a sandbox escape hatch baked in. When a command is blocked by the sandbox, Claude will attempt to execute the same thing without the sandbox. The only difference is that it is supposed to prompt you... But this feels like one bug away from just sandbox escape.

comments.author: altano
comments.text: You can disable that in your settings and only allow sandbox execution, but yes your general point still stands.

comments.author: myme
comments.text:
I’ve been experimenting with a similar approach myself, perhaps a bit more all-in on nix tooling: https://github.com/myme/jaillm

Using https://git.sr.ht/~alexdavid/jail.nix to automate bubblewrap in a nix-friendly way.

Being able to pull in the entire development environment (devShell) along with any other required tools feels very powerful while quite ergonomic. While I should note it’s still just an experiment so assessing how to make it more secure without compromising functionality is something that needs more effort. That said, I think it’s the direction I’d like to see working with coding agents going forwards.

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text: I guess this works, but to me Slopus falls into the "personal tool" category, so I'm not going to add it along with sandboxing to a project I might be collaboratively working with other people, or I forked to submit a PR. There's also trust issues - I enjoy projects having flake.nix as I don't need to spend any time to set up dev env, but I don't necessarily trust them. So I want to sandbox with my own code. That's why I do it on my system's/user's Nix flake level.

comments.author: myme
comments.text:
I understand. My intention with jaillm was to be able to pull in whatever permutations of software that makes sense for any given project. The default is to not pull in anything but the LLMs, so no implicit integration. Adding deps from the repo requires explicitly stating so by importing expressions from a flake or default.nix import. I currently only do so with a few projects me or the team maintain. I also don’t track jaillm.nix in version control as I’m the sole user.

It’s nice to see alternative approaches and might consider having a user global env too.

comments.author: vbernat
comments.text: I am using something similar: https://github.com/vincentbernat/zshrc/blob/master/rc/alias.zsh#L182. I am still wondering if there is something less "opt-in" for isolation, maybe SELinux, but with less hassle.

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text:
I suspect there's going to be a lot of tooling like that. It's just a good idea, IMO.

I thought about it for a while: how generic this can be, and it seems to me that various users will have varying level of requirements and it all will work best if the users very tightly controls and fully understand their sandboxing. So for starter I have a very custom and "minimum-abstraction" level solution tailored for myself.

But any solution is probably good enough, and better than nothing, including the built-in sandboxing. Whatever works.

comments.author: lvl
comments.text:
Thanks! I'll use this isolation script for other use cases, as I do see advantages for build processes that are not happening in my Nix build sandbox.

I did notice however, that if you do share ~/.config as read-only, tokens and other stuff might leak, depending on what you have there. This would still incur really high costs for you if malware picks it up. I'll adapt your isolation script to be more granular on those .config entries.

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text:
I did notice however, that if you do share ~/.config as read-only, tokens and other stuff might leak, depending on what you have there. This would still incur really high costs for you if malware picks it up. I'll adapt your isolation script to be more granular on those .config entries.


That's a good point. I should  make it more granular as well. Ideally tools would keep secrets in some mutable dir like ~/.local/state/ so the config itself can be widely shared, but I bet a lot of tools don't do it this way. I probably just want to mount the few sub-dirs for tools I actually need in the dev sandbox.

comments.author: ashishb
comments.text:
bubblewrap does not work on Mac OS.
sandbox-exec has been deprecated

$ man sandbox-exec
SANDBOX-EXEC(1)                                   General Commands Manual                                   SANDBOX-EXEC(1)

NAME
     sandbox-exec – execute within a sandbox (DEPRECATED)

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text:
My opinion: these battery times are not worth suffering all the shortcomings of OS optimized for being an appliance. Just use Linux. Or like me - learn to work on Linux via ssh, and potentially keep shiny MacOS laptop as a nice remote client.

In my teams I support building systems, CI, dev env for all developers, which is Linux and MacOS users. MacOS requires constant troubleshooting and fixing, and it is largely a blackbox with Apple breaking dev stuff every minor update. IMO one has to make up their mind. Either their computer is an appliance, or it's a tool.

comments.author: viraptor
comments.text: That deprecation is irrelevant in practice. The recommended app sandbox is extremely simple and doesn't cover many interesting cases. Basically all system services on MacOS are using sandbox-exec. That functionality has been deprecated for years, but has no real replacement - it's not going anywhere.

comments.author: ashishb
comments.text:
That functionality has been deprecated for years, but has no real replacement - it's not going anywhere.


SIP broke many features as well.
There is no real requirement for an alternative to be provided.

comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
sandbox-exec provides a lot of defence in depth for the current system tools. (And large apps like common browsers) I don't believe they'd just drop that. Especially not with the recent interest in enterprise deployments - they need some real sandboxing to exist.

SIP was an extra feature, not removing something that exists, even if it broke things.
